question:
Patient note:
A 48-year-old man is reviewed in the pre-operative holding bay this morning for a planned laparoscopic interval appendectomy after an uncomplicated induction of general anesthesia. Three weeks ago he presented to the emergency department with fever, rigors, and diffuse abdominal discomfort; computed tomography at that time revealed a perforated gangrenous appendix with a 4-cm peri-cecal phlegmon and early loculated fluid, and he met systemic inflammatory response criteria and was diagnosed with sepsis secondary to the intra-abdominal infection. He was managed non-operatively with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and CT-guided drainage, defervesced within forty-eight hours, and completed an additional twelve days of ertapenem through a single-lumen power-injectable peripherally inserted catheter placed in the right basilic vein. The line remains in situ today, covered by an intact occlusive dressing, and is currently running 0.9 % saline at 50 mL/h pending the start of anesthesia. Because of persistent low-grade ileus during that admission he has spent the majority of each day reclining—effectively on bed rest—transferring from bed only for brief assisted walks to the bathroom; nursing flow sheets document fewer than 150 cumulative steps over the last seventy-two hours, and he reports feeling “deconditioned” when he tries to stand for longer than a minute. He denies new cough, purulent sputum, pleuritic chest pain, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, palpitations, or exertional chest tightness. His medical history is otherwise notable only for long-standing superficial venous dilation over both lower legs diagnosed in his thirties after years of retail work that required prolonged standing; he continues to wear below-knee graduated compression hose for aching along the course of the great saphenous distribution but notes no discoloration, tenderness, or calf fullness today. He has never experienced a blood clot, has not taken chronic anticoagulation, and is unaware of thromboembolic events among first-degree relatives. There is no history of major operations in the past year, no casts, splints, or fractures of the lower extremities, no spinal cord or head injuries, no strokes, no chronic lung disease, and no malignancy. He takes lisinopril 10 mg daily for well-controlled hypertension, as-needed acetaminophen, and a men’s multivitamin; he does not use estrogen products, glucocorticoids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or nicotine. Alcohol intake is limited to two beers on the weekend, and he denies recreational drug use. Review of systems is otherwise negative for weight loss, night sweats, diarrhea, hematochezia, dysuria, or rash. On examination he is supine in bed, conversant, and appears younger than his stated age. Vital signs: temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 128/74 mm Hg, heart rate 78 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98 % on room air. Body mass index is 27 kg/m². Jugular venous pulsation is not elevated, carotid upstrokes are brisk, and peripheral pulses are 2+ and symmetric. Cardiac auscultation reveals a crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Breath sounds are vesicular throughout with no wheezes or crackles. The abdomen is soft with mild residual tenderness in the right lower quadrant around the healed drain site; no guarding, rebound, or organomegaly is present, and bowel sounds are active. The right upper arm dressing overlies the catheter insertion site, which is clean, dry, and without erythema or induration. Lower-extremity inspection shows multiple tortuous bluish veins along the posteromedial calves but no pitting edema, erythema, or focal warmth; calf circumferences are symmetric, and gentle dorsiflexion elicits no discomfort. Neurologic evaluation demonstrates full strength and intact sensation in all extremities; gait is not assessed because the patient has been instructed to remain on the stretcher. Skin is intact without ulcers or ecchymoses. Pre-operative laboratories drawn through the catheter yesterday reveal hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, hematocrit 42 %, platelet count 247 × 10⁹/L, white blood cells 7.2 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, creatinine 0.92 mg/dL, AST 22 U/L, ALT 18 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, fasting glucose 96 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.4 s with an INR of 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 30 s. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram demonstrates normal sinus rhythm without ST-T abnormalities, and a chest radiograph obtained five days ago to evaluate line position shows clear lung fields and the catheter tip terminating at the cavo-atrial junction. Airway assessment reveals Mallampati class II view, adequate mouth opening, full neck extension, and normal thyromental distance; no loose teeth or cervical spine limitations are noted. The surgical team anticipates a one- to two-hour operative time with three 5-mm trocar sites, minimal blood loss, and discharge from the hospital on post-operative day one if recovery proceeds as expected. Sequential compression sleeves are ordered but have not yet been applied, and pharmacologic prophylaxis will be initiated after fascial closure in accordance with institutional policy once hemostasis is confirmed.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini perioperative VTE score adds weighted risk factors present before surgery:
- Age 48 (41–60 years): 1 point.
- BMI 27 kg/m² (>25): 1 point.
- Visible varicose veins: 1 point.
- Sepsis three weeks ago (within one month): 1 point.
- Current bed rest with only brief bathroom walks: 1 point. This counts current bed rest rather than assigning 2 points for confinement exceeding 72 hours; the quantified mobility record covers 72 hours.
- Indwelling PICC with a central tip: 2 points.
- Planned laparoscopic operation lasting 60–120 minutes (>45 minutes): 2 points.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 9.
Final answer: 9
